name: southern style cornbread
instructions:
From Daniel Gritzer, Serious Eats — 'Southern-Style Unsweetened Cornbread'. A LESS SWEET / LESS CAKE-LIKE alternative to sweet-potato-cornbread (which reads more like a cake). Cornmeal-forward, no wheat flour, minimal sweetness. TESTED — several ratios adjusted from Gritzer's original (see COOK NOTES).

SERVES 12. Makes ~2.5 lb. 12-inch cast-iron skillet (Gritzer's spec; 8-inch mostly works with the adjusted-down ratios — see COOK NOTES).

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 15 oz (3 cups) STONE-GROUND CORNMEAL (see notes — the cornmeal quality is the whole dish)
- 1/2 to 1 tsp kosher salt (Gritzer's 2 tsp is too much — see COOK NOTES)
- 2 tsp baking powder
- 3/4 tsp baking soda
- 1 tbsp (3 tsp) sugar (Gritzer frames this as optional; in practice, 1 tbsp is right — see COOK NOTES)
- 1 cup buttermilk (Gritzer says 2 1/2 cups — way too much; see COOK NOTES)
- 3 eggs
- 1/2 cup (8 tbsp) UNSALTED BUTTER, melted, divided (Gritzer says 12 tbsp / 1 1/2 sticks — too much; see COOK NOTES). Or lard / bacon fat.

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. Place a well-seasoned 12-inch CAST IRON SKILLET on the center rack of the oven and preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). The skillet preheats WITH the oven — this is what produces the crisp edges (see notes).
2. Meanwhile, in a large bowl, whisk the cornmeal with salt, baking powder, baking soda, and sugar (if using).
3. In a separate bowl, whisk the buttermilk with the eggs until homogenous. Whisking constantly, drizzle in all but 1 tablespoon of the melted butter.
4. Whisk the liquid ingredients into the dry ingredients JUST until thoroughly mixed. Avoid over-mixing.
5. Pour the remaining 1 tablespoon melted butter into the preheated skillet and carefully swirl to coat the bottom and sides.
6. Scrape the batter into the prepared skillet, smoothing the top gently with a rubber spatula. Bake until lightly browned on top and a skewer inserted into the center comes out clean — about 45 minutes.
7. Let cool for about 15 minutes in the skillet, then serve warm.

Doesn't keep well — eat fresh (see notes).
notes:
Source: Daniel Gritzer, Serious Eats — 'Southern-Style Unsweetened Cornbread' (November 2015, updated February 2025). TESTED — see COOK NOTES for what worked and what didn't from Gritzer's exact recipe.

=== JOURNEY / EVOLVING VIEW ON HYDRATION ===

My stance on this recipe has moved. Documenting the arc so future me remembers.

FIRST READ OF GRITZER'S RECIPE — SKEPTICAL OF OVERHYDRATION: on paper, 2 1/2 cups buttermilk + 12 tbsp butter for 3 cups cornmeal read as way too much liquid. Cut buttermilk to 1 cup and butter to 1/2 cup (8 tbsp) — kept everything else at Gritzer's scale (3 cups cornmeal, 3 eggs). Felt confident this would be tighter and better.

FIRST COOK OF THE ADJUSTED VERSION — CAME OUT EGGY + A BIT DRY: exactly the failure modes you'd expect from under-hydration. The 3 eggs weren't proportionally over the top in Gritzer's original — they were sitting inside a lot of buttermilk and butter that softened their weight on the palate. Cutting the buttermilk and butter without also cutting the eggs left the eggs dominating the flavor. And less total liquid + less fat = drier crumb.

SECOND REFERENCE — RACHEL BALLARD (FEAST AND FARM) CORROBORATES GRITZER: Ballard's 'Southern Cornbread' recipe (aggressively no-sugar, self-rising cornmeal mix, 9-inch cast iron, veg oil crust) lands 2 cups cornmeal to 2 eggs to 1 3/4 cups buttermilk. That's roughly 1:1 cornmeal:buttermilk by volume — the SAME ratio Gritzer's original hits when you scale down. Two independent southern-cornbread references converging on the same wet ratio is a real signal I underweighted in the first pass.

CURRENT WORKING HYPOTHESIS: my skepticism of overhydration was wrong. The southern-cornbread tradition wants a WETTER batter than my instinct wanted to allow. What I read as 'too wet' when reading the recipe cold turns out to be what actually delivers a moist, non-eggy crumb.

NEXT COOK — DIRECTION: bump buttermilk back toward 1:1 cornmeal:buttermilk (roughly 3 cups buttermilk for 3 cups cornmeal, or scale down to 2 eggs + 1 3/4 cups buttermilk per Ballard). Butter can probably stay reduced (~1/2 cup is close to Ballard's total-fat number), but the buttermilk was the load-bearing under-adjustment. See 2-EGG COMPARISON table below for the exact three-way ratio spread.

=== COOK NOTES — RATIOS ADJUSTED FROM GRITZER'S ORIGINAL ===

Gritzer got some things right and some wrong. What I've landed on:

- 3 CUPS CORNMEAL : 3 EGGS : 1 TBSP SUGAR — right, keep as-is. Could also push to 2 EGGS + 2 TBSP SUGAR as an alternative variation (untested that specific swap, but plausible).
- BUTTER + BUTTERMILK — WAY TOO MUCH LIQUID as written. Gritzer's 12 tbsp butter + 2.5 cups buttermilk overshoots. Cutting to 1/2 CUP BUTTER + 1 CUP BUTTERMILK is basically optimal.
- SALT — GRITZER'S 2 TSP IS TOO MUCH. Cut to 1/2 to 1 tsp. Even 1 tsp felt like too much on the last cook; err toward 1/2.
- LEAVENERS — kept as-written (2 tsp baking powder + 3/4 tsp baking soda). Doesn't rise much regardless (see below).
- SUGAR IS NOT OPTIONAL IN PRACTICE — Gritzer frames it as optional (only for mass-market cornmeal), but I've landed on 1 tbsp being the right amount even with good cornmeal. Keep the sugar.

=== PROPORTIONAL SCALE-DOWN — GRITZER'S ORIGINAL RATIOS AT 1 CUP BUTTERMILK (WANT TO TRY) ===

A straight proportional scale of Gritzer's original recipe (× 0.4) to hit 1 cup of buttermilk/yogurt. Different from the adjusted ratios above — this version preserves Gritzer's INTERNAL ratios but shrinks the whole recipe. Untested; want to try to compare against the adjusted version.

| ingredient | Gritzer's original | Scaled (× 0.4) |
|---|---|---|
| Cornmeal | 3 cups (15 oz) | 1.2 cups (~6 oz) |
| Kosher salt | 2 tsp | 0.8 tsp (~3/4 tsp) |
| Baking powder | 2 tsp | 0.8 tsp (~3/4 tsp) |
| Baking soda | 3/4 tsp | 0.3 tsp (~1/4 tsp + a pinch) |
| Sugar | 3 tsp / 1 tbsp | 1.2 tsp (~1 tsp+) |
| Buttermilk (or yogurt) | 2 1/2 cups | 1 cup |
| Eggs | 3 | 1.2 eggs (1 large + a splash, or just 1) |
| Butter, melted | 12 tbsp / 1 1/2 sticks | 4.8 tbsp (~5 tbsp) |

DIVERGENCES FROM MY ADJUSTED VERSION (see COOK NOTES above):
- Cornmeal: this scale gives 1.2 cups; my adjusted version keeps 3 cups. My version is much more cornmeal-dense per cup of buttermilk.
- Butter: this gives ~5 tbsp; my adjusted version is 8 tbsp (butter-heavier per buttermilk).
- Sugar: this gives ~1 tsp; my adjusted version is 1 tbsp (sugar-heavier per buttermilk).
- Salt: this gives ~3/4 tsp; my adjusted version is 1/2 to 1 tsp — roughly matches.
- Leaveners: this gives 3/4 tsp powder + 1/4 tsp soda; my adjusted version keeps 2 tsp + 3/4 tsp — much more leavened per buttermilk. Worth revisiting: I noted the adjusted version 'doesn't rise much', but maybe I'm just under-leavened relative to the amount of dry ingredient it has to lift.

=== 2-EGG COMPARISON — GRITZER vs RACHEL BALLARD (FEAST AND FARM) vs MY HANDROLLED ===

Three southern-cornbread paths side-by-side at the 2-egg scale. Gritzer's is × 2/3 of his original; Ballard's is her actual recipe (Feast and Farm — no-sugar southern; self-rising cornmeal mix); mine is my handrolled version (3 eggs, 1 cup buttermilk, 1/2 cup butter, 3 cups cornmeal) scaled × 2/3 to 2 eggs.

| ingredient | Gritzer × 2/3 | Rachel Ballard | Mine × 2/3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cornmeal | 2 cups stone-ground | 2 cups self-rising mix | 2 cups stone-ground |
| Eggs | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| Buttermilk | 1 2/3 cups | 1 3/4 cups | 2/3 cup |
| Salt | 1 1/3 tsp | (in mix) | 1/3 – 2/3 tsp |
| Baking powder | 1 1/3 tsp | (in mix) | 1 1/3 tsp |
| Baking soda | 1/2 tsp | none | 1/2 tsp |
| Sugar | 2 tsp | none | 2 tsp |
| Fat IN batter | 8 tbsp butter | 2 tbsp veg oil | ~5 tbsp butter |
| Fat IN skillet | ~1 tbsp (of above) | 1/4 cup veg oil (crust-maker) | ~1 tbsp (Gritzer's rule) |
| Total fat | 8 tbsp butter | ~6 tbsp veg oil | ~5 tbsp butter |
| Skillet size | 12-inch | 9-inch | 8-inch |
| Oven | 375°F, ~45 min | 400°F, 25-30 min | 375°F, ~45 min |

BIG DIVERGENCE — BUTTERMILK: both Gritzer and Ballard converge on roughly 1:1 cornmeal:buttermilk by volume. My handrolled version at 2-egg scale is about 3:1 cornmeal:buttermilk — much drier. Two independent southern-cornbread references landing on ~1:1 vs my 3:1 is a real signal.

FAT: my handrolled × 2/3 lands ~5 tbsp butter — close to Ballard's ~6 tbsp total, notably less than Gritzer's 8 tbsp. My fat number is defensible.

SUGAR: I'm at 2 tsp (Gritzer proportional); Ballard has zero. If you want the strict-southern read, drop the sugar.

=== FIRST-COOK RESULT — 'EGGY' + BIT DRY (POINTS AT UNDER-BUTTERMILK / UNDER-BUTTER) ===

First cook of my handrolled version (3 eggs, 1 cup buttermilk, 1/2 cup butter, 3 cups cornmeal): came out EGGY tasting and A BIT DRY. Consistent with the comparison table observation above — lowering buttermilk and butter relative to eggs left the eggs proportionally dominant on the palate, and reduced the liquid + fat below the wetness needed for a moist crumb.

DIAGNOSTIC PATH FOR NEXT ATTEMPT: either bump buttermilk toward Gritzer/Ballard's ~1:1 cornmeal:buttermilk ratio (would be ~3 cups buttermilk for 3 cups cornmeal), OR scale eggs down (to 2 eggs) while keeping the same buttermilk. Or both. The eggy taste is probably eggs-per-buttermilk being too high; the dryness is probably total-liquid + fat being too low.

=== DOESN'T RISE MUCH ===

General observation: this cornbread doesn't rise much regardless of leavener quantity. Don't expect a tall fluffy loaf; expect a dense-ish flat-topped bake. That's what it is.

=== SKILLET SIZE — 12-INCH PER GRITZER, BUT 8-INCH MOSTLY WORKS ===

Gritzer wrote the recipe for a 12-inch cast iron skillet. With the ADJUSTED ratios above (less butter, less buttermilk), most (but not all) of the batter fits in an 8-inch skillet. I can see why Gritzer went for the 12-inch — the batter volume is a bit too much for 8-inch — but 8-inch is workable if you accept some overflow or scale down slightly.

=== CORNMEAL QUALITY IS THE WHOLE DISH ===

Gritzer is emphatic: the cornmeal itself has the single biggest impact on the final cornbread. High-quality stone-ground cornmeal (a variety of textures from floury to coarse) is what produces a light, fluffy bread with crackly bits of corn grit and real corn flavor. Mass-market industrial cornmeal (uniform grind from underripe corn) doesn't work — reads flat and 'sub-zero on the sweetness scale'.

RECOMMENDED SOURCES (from Gritzer): Anson Mills, Old Mill of Guilford, Nora Mill. Order online or seek out a local mill.

=== SUGAR — 1 TBSP IS RIGHT (NOT OPTIONAL IN PRACTICE) ===

Gritzer frames sugar as optional (only for mass-market cornmeal). In practice — even with good stone-ground cornmeal — 1 TBSP per 3 cups cornmeal is right. Keep the sugar. The dish is still 'unsweetened' in the sense that it's not a sweet cornbread; the sugar just balances the flavor. Skipping it makes the finished bread read incomplete.

This is why the file rename dropped the 'unsweetened' framing: the recipe technically isn't unsweetened, and the sugar isn't optional; the iron-skillet + cornmeal-forward technique is the more distinctive feature.

=== NO WHEAT FLOUR — SOUTHERN STYLE, OPPOSITE OF NORTHERN ===

This is the Southern-style shape: cornmeal only, no wheat flour, no (or minimal) sugar. Northern-style cornbread uses wheat flour to correct for coarse industrial grind and sugar to compensate for less-ripe corn. Different dish. If you want a sweeter/cake-like cornbread, reach for sweet-potato-cornbread instead — that one is explicitly more of a cake.

=== PREHEAT THE CAST IRON SKILLET — CRISP EDGES ===

Put the empty cast iron skillet in the oven while it preheats. Pour the batter into the already-hot skillet. This is what produces the crisp edges the recipe is known for. Skip this step and you get a softer-edged bread that's fine but not the same dish.

=== FAT — BUTTER, OR LARD / BACON FAT ===

Melted butter is the default. LARD or BACON FAT also work well (per Gritzer) — push the register more traditional-southern. Same quantity.

=== DOESN'T KEEP WELL — EAT FRESH ===

Cornbread loses its texture as it cools past the day-of window. Eat while fresh. Day-old cornbread is still useful for dressing / stuffing applications (per Gritzer + the comments) but the standalone eating experience degrades.

=== SIBLING RECIPE — SWEET POTATO CORNBREAD ===

sweet-potato-cornbread (Anita Spring Councel, Southern Roots) is the sweeter, cake-like cornbread in this cookbook. Includes wheat flour, sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, orange zest, and mashed sweet potato. Different register entirely.

When to reach for which:
- SWEET POTATO CORNBREAD: sweet, cake-like, pairs with cream cheese frosting or savory ham/prosciutto.
- THIS RECIPE (SOUTHERN UNSWEETENED): cornmeal-forward, dense corn flavor, savory register, meant to go with beans/greens/chili or under a savory main.
